title: Decidability of regular-path view determinacy
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal:
Is there a deterministic algorithm that halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), finitely many finite automata \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\) defining view queries \(V_1,\ldots,V_m\), and a finite automaton \(B_0\) defining a target query \(Q\), and decides whether
\[
\forall\text{ finite }\Sigma\text{-labeled graph databases }D,D':\quad
\left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^m V_i(D)=V_i(D')\right)\Longrightarrow Q(D)=Q(D')?
\]
The queries return endpoint pairs of matching finite directed walks, as defined below. The universal database quantification is part of the property to decide; databases themselves are not supplied to the algorithm. There is no running-time bound.

source_formulation.text: The 2015 related-work passage asks whether classical regular-path-query determinacy is decidable and what rewriting language could express it. This card selects the finite-database decision branch as an announced editorial default after an optional scope question. It does not treat the second branch as an independently specified target.
source_formulation.caption: Francis, ICDT 2015, related work on pp.45–46.

why: View answers may hide different underlying graphs. Determinacy asks whether that hidden variation can ever change a target answer, a global static-analysis problem even though each individual regular path query is effectively evaluable.
status_note: Resolved negatively by Głuch–Marcinkowski–Ostropolski-Nalewaja (LICS 2018), Theorem I.1, explicitly for finite graph databases. The 2026 primary discussion independently retains that endpoint result while proving positive statements for whole-walk outputs. The review checked the theorem and model scope rather than independently formalizing its proof.

progress.text: The source records decidability as unknown for general regular-path views and queries.
Theorem I.1 establishes undecidability, explicitly including finite database structures.
The newer whole-walk-semantics paper confirms the classical endpoint lower bound while proving different decidable variants.

category_assignment.reason: The actual property is view determinacy and rewriting of graph database queries.

importance.reason: View determinacy expresses whether released or materialized information suffices for every possible underlying database. Its decidability boundary connects query optimization, rewriting and information disclosure; the historical RPQ problem is a basic instance of that boundary.

sentences: The input specifies regular path queries representing a collection of views and one target query.
Each query returns pairs of endpoints connected by a matching directed walk.
Determinacy requires every two finite databases with the same view answers to have the same target answer.
The question of deciding that property is known to be undecidable.
The archived decision target is distinct from monotone determinacy and from newer semantics that return entire walks.

definitions:
A graph database over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) consists of a finite domain of vertex names and, for each symbol \(a\in\Sigma\), a binary relation \(R_a\) on that domain. An ordered pair in \(R_a\) is a directed edge labeled \(a\). Loops are allowed, and two vertices may be joined by edges of several labels. Each relation is a set, so identical edges are not repeated. Vertex names can be taken from the nonnegative integers. Two databases in the determinacy test need not have the same edge relations or even the same domain; their returned pairs are compared as sets of names.

A nondeterministic finite automaton consists of a finite set of states, initial and accepting state subsets, and transitions labeled by alphabet symbols or the empty word. Its language consists of the finite words labeling runs from initial to accepting states, ignoring empty-word transitions. Automata, alphabet symbols, state sets and transitions are explicitly listed in binary. All finite alphabet sizes, state counts and numbers of views are permitted; no language or view is fixed in advance. Using regular expressions instead gives an effectively equivalent decidability question.

For an automaton \(B\), its regular path query returns the binary relation
\[
Q_B(D)=\{(x,y):\exists\ell\ge0\ \exists v_0=x,\ldots,v_\ell=y\ \exists a_1\cdots a_\ell\in L(B)\ \forall j\in[\ell],\ (v_{j-1},v_j)\in R_{a_j}\}.
\]
All vertices on the walk belong to the domain. They and its edges may repeat. The empty walk contributes \((x,x)\) when the empty word belongs to the language. Only endpoint pairs are returned, not the walk, its length, its number of realizations or a shortest-path witness. The outputs use set semantics.

Put \(V_i=Q_{B_i}\) and \(Q=Q_{B_0}\). Determinacy means that any two finite databases agreeing on all view relations also agree on the target relation. No monotonicity condition on the function taking view relations to the target is assumed, and the views are exact, rather than incomplete lower or upper approximations. The proposed decider must answer both positive and negative instances correctly and terminate on both.

The target selects the decidability branch of the historical source passage. It does not ask for a language in which to express rewritings, for monotone determinacy, or for recovery of full walks. It also does not concern the source paper's separate restricted family of single-letter unions of path-length queries. A decision procedure for one of those variants would not decide this problem.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the stated total decider. A negative answer can be established by an effective reduction from a proved undecidable problem, covering the finite-database endpoint semantics above. Merely giving a complexity lower bound, a result for infinite databases only, or an algorithm for monotone determinacy does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: The historical passage concerns general regular path queries, whereas its surrounding paper studies a narrower path-length setting. The two scopes must not be conflated.

Theorem I.1 gives undecidability and explicitly covers finite databases. The finite version is co-recursively-enumerable complete: finite counterexample databases can be enumerated, but determinacy has no total decider.
The 2026 positive results return entire matching walks under specified semantics. They do not reverse the endpoint-determinacy lower bound selected here.
